title: How 10,000 Years of Potato Farming Reshaped Human DNA in the Andes
excerpt: A landmark genetic study reveals that Indigenous Andeans carry the world's highest number of starch-digestion genes — an evolutionary adaptation driven by thousands of years of potato cultivation.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indigenous Andeans average 10 AMY1 gene copies, surpassing other populations in starch digestion capacity.
  • Natural selection favored high AMY1 copy numbers 6,000 to 10,000 years ago with potato domestication.
  • Individuals with 10+ AMY1 copies gained a 1.24% survival advantage per generation over centuries.
  • The study analyzed genomic data from 3,723 individuals across 85 global populations.

  • Indigenous Andeans in Peru carry an average of 10 copies of the AMY1 gene — two to four more than any other population studied — giving them the world's highest starch-digestion capacity.
  • Natural selection began favouring individuals with high AMY1 copy numbers roughly 6,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with the domestication of potatoes in the Andean highlands.
  • Those with 10 or more AMY1 copies gained a 1.24% survival or reproductive advantage per generation, a small edge that compounded across hundreds of generations.
  • The study, published in Nature Communications, analysed genomic data from over 3,700 individuals across 85 populations worldwide.

The potato may be the world's most unassuming staple food, but a landmark study has revealed that this humble tuber didn't merely feed ancient Andean civilisations — it fundamentally rewired their DNA.

Research published in the journal Nature Communications by scientists at UCLA and the University at Buffalo has found that Indigenous communities in Peru's Andean highlands carry the highest known number of starch-digestion genes of any human population on Earth. The discovery provides some of the strongest evidence yet that human diets can drive genetic evolution over relatively short timescales.

The AMY1 Advantage

At the centre of the findings is a gene called AMY1, which produces salivary amylase — an enzyme that begins breaking down starch in the mouth. Most people worldwide carry about seven copies of AMY1. But the Quechua-speaking Andean populations studied by the researchers averaged 10 copies, a significant outlier.

"Biologists have long suspected that different groups of humans have evolved genetic adaptations in response to their diets, but there are very few cases where the evidence is this strong," said Omer Gokcumen, professor of biological sciences at the University at Buffalo and co-author of the study.

The team analysed genomic data from 3,723 individuals representing 85 populations across the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia. The sample included 81 people of Indigenous Andean ancestry in Peru. The Quechua speakers consistently showed the highest AMY1 copy numbers of any group.

When Potatoes Drove Evolution

The timing of the genetic shift is what makes the finding so compelling. The researchers traced the increase in AMY1 copies to roughly 6,000 to 10,000 years ago — the same period when Indigenous communities high in the Andes Mountains first domesticated the potato.

Using ultra-long-read DNA sequencing technology, the team demonstrated that recombination events in the genome produced expanded clusters of AMY1 copies. Natural selection then favoured these high-copy variants as potatoes became a dietary staple.

The advantage was modest but persistent: individuals with 10 or more AMY1 copies gained a 1.24% survival or reproductive advantage per generation, according to the study. Over hundreds of generations, even that small edge produced a large cumulative effect on the population.

"It is a wonderful case of culture shaping biology."

— Omer Gokcumen, University at Buffalo, to Reuters

"Evolution is chiselling a sculpture, not constructing a building," Gokcumen explained. "It's not as if Indigenous Andeans gained additional AMY1 copies once they started eating potatoes. Instead, those with lower copy numbers were eliminated from the population over time, and the ones with higher copy numbers remained."

Ruling Out Other Explanations

The researchers had to account for a complicating factor: the catastrophic decline in Indigenous populations following European contact in the 15th century, which caused disease, famine, and a rapid loss of genetic diversity. Could this population bottleneck — rather than natural selection — have disproportionately removed individuals with lower AMY1 counts?

The ultra-long DNA sequencing showed that high AMY1 copy numbers rose in frequency in the Andes thousands of years before Europeans arrived. A direct comparison reinforced the finding: Indigenous Peruvians averaged 10 copies of AMY1, compared to just six for the Maya — an Indigenous Mexican population with shared evolutionary history but without a tradition of potato farming.

"This direct comparison is one of the major reasons why we think their high number of AMY1 copies did not evolve just by chance but instead linked to their long history of eating potatoes," said Luane Landau, a PhD student in Gokcumen's lab and joint first author of the study.

What This Means for Modern Diets

The findings raise provocative questions about the relationship between genes and diet in the modern world. For most of human history, people ate what their ancestors had eaten for millennia. Today, globalised food systems mean that virtually everyone eats potatoes — and french fries — regardless of whether their genes are optimised for starch digestion.

"There could come a day when our diets are personalised according to our DNA," Gokcumen said. The research suggests that people with fewer AMY1 copies may metabolise starchy foods less efficiently, with potential implications for understanding obesity, diabetes, and metabolic health.

"Our metabolic pathways are not simply a product of that Paleolithic past," said Abigail Bigham, associate professor of anthropology at UCLA and co-author. "Human populations have responded and evolved to changing food conditions within the last 10,000 years."

A Broader Legacy

Peru remains home to between 3,000 and 4,000 varieties of potato — far beyond the smooth russets and pale Maris Pipers found on Western supermarket shelves. These come in shades of purple, pink, red, and black, a living testament to millennia of cultivation by Andean communities.

The study, which involved collaborators from the University of Kansas, Penn State, the University of Pennsylvania, Syracuse University, and Cayetano Heredia University in Peru, was supported by the National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, and the Leakey Foundation.
